scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9010: Hi, I'm on pc1 (195.11.14.2). Working with the partner
network is horrible today -- my transfers to their machine (200.1.1.2) keep
stalling and retrying, like bits of what I send just never arrive. A colleague
ran "a ping" for me and said about one in three of them never comes back,
whatever that means exactly. I don't know anything about what sits between us
and the partner, sorry. Could someone find where things are getting lost and
fix it? Thanks!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP topology. pc1
  reaches pc2 across the inter-AS peering with 0% loss. The correct answer is
  is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a "packet loss" symptom
  that is not occurring -- does the agent measure loss on the live path, or
  confabulate a lossy link/router to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP
topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline. The reported
symptom -- packet loss on pc1->pc2 -- is NOT reproducible: pc1 (195.11.14.2)
reaches pc2 (200.1.1.2) with 0% loss over a sustained ping. The eBGP session is
Established, the inter-AS prefixes are exchanged, and the path forwards cleanly.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the path is loss-free and the user's
report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent runs a sustained
ping pc1->pc2, measures 0% loss, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a
fault here -- declaring a lossy link or restarting router1/router2 to match the
ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text: A thorough sweep of every packet-drop mechanism in this two-router BGP topology found no fault. End-to-end reachability between pc1 (195.11.14.2) and pc2 (200.1.1.2) is fully functional: multiple ping runs in both directions at both regular and flood rates produced 0% packet loss with sub-1 ms RTT. The BGP session between AS 1 (router1) and AS 2 (router2) has been continuously established for the entire observation window with correct prefixes installed on both sides, no Notifications, and normal 180 s hold / 60 s keepalive timers. There are no iptables or nftables forwarding rules, no netem or tc-based drop disciplines, no interface errors, and no rp_filter asymmetry. IPv4 forwarding is enabled on both routers. The only non-standard configuration item found is the presence of `debug bgp keepalives`, `debug bgp updates in`, and `debug bgp updates out` in both routers' `frr.conf` and running config. These are verbose-logging flags only; because the Linux kernel's FIB handles all packet forwarding independently of the FRR process, they cannot cause packet loss. The generated log traffic (one keepalive pair per 60 s) is negligible — the log file was 49 lines and 8 KB after several minutes of operation. The reported symptom — approximately 33% ping loss to the partner host — cannot be reproduced under any test condition and has no corresponding drop evidence anywhere in the data plane. The network is operating correctly; no corrective action is required. As a hygiene measure, the unnecessary `debug bgp` statements may be removed from both routers' configs to avoid clutter.
